item.title: Getting back into chess at 30
item.description:
Restarted chess seriously in January after a decade of dabbling. Current Lichess rapid: 1970. Target: 2200 by year-end.

What’s working

  • Puzzle rush, 10 minutes a day. No analysis, just pattern drilling.
  • One annotated master game per day. Slow, notes on paper. I’ve learned more from 40 games this way than from 500 online blitz.
  • Post-mortem every rated loss. No excuses, no engine — first I identify the moment I went wrong, then I turn on the engine.

What isn’t

  • Blitz. It’s fun but it’s ruining my calculation discipline. Limiting to one session a week.
  • Openings obsession. I was building a repertoire like it was a hobby in itself. Now I play two openings on each side, and I study positions arising from them, not openings in the abstract.

Books I’m actually reading

  1. My System — Nimzowitsch. Occasionally dated, structurally essential.
  2. Think Like a Grandmaster — Kotov. The “analysis tree” discipline is worth the book on its own.
  3. Pump Up Your Rating — Axel Smith. Practical, no-nonsense.

The single biggest lesson so far: sit on your hands. Almost every blunder in my loss database comes from a move I could have spent thirty more seconds on.

item.description:

item.title: Binary Search — and how I kept getting it wrong
item.description:
Binary search is the algorithm I’ve “known” the longest and written incorrectly the most times. The issue is never the idea. It’s the off-by-one.

The canonical bug

# Wrong on the edges
def bs(nums, target):
 lo, hi = 0, len(nums)
 while lo < hi:
 mid = (lo + hi) // 2
 if nums[mid] == target:
 return mid
 elif nums[mid] < target:
 lo = mid # ← infinite loop
 else:
 hi = mid
 return -1

lo = mid without + 1 stalls when lo + 1 == hi.

item.title: Outer Wilds
item.description:
Finally played Outer Wilds. It lives up to the reputation — probably the purest expression of curiosity-as-gameplay I’ve ever seen. No combat, no upgrades, no gear checks. Just you, a ship, and a solar system full of things that deserve to be understood.

Spoilers would genuinely hurt the experience, so I’ll just say: every “aha” moment lands, and the structure of the final act is audacious.

item.title: Git worktrees changed how I work
item.description:
I avoided git worktree for years because “stash and switch branches” felt fine. It wasn’t fine; I’d just never felt the alternative.

The pitch: instead of switching branches in place (which nukes your working directory and forces you to rebuild, re-run tests, restart the dev server), you have multiple branches checked out in sibling directories, all sharing the same .git.

git worktree add ../repo-feature-x feature-x
cd ../repo-feature-x
# separate working tree, separate node_modules if you want,
# separate everything except the .git store

Where this wins

  • Reviewing a PR without losing your current branch’s build state.
  • Comparing behavior across branches with two running dev servers.
  • Long-running tasks (a heavy test suite, a migration) that you don’t want to interrupt just to fix a typo on main.
  • Agent-based workflows — if you let an AI agent work on a branch, you don’t want it touching the files your editor is sitting in.

Gotchas

  • node_modules isn’t shared by default. Solvable with pnpm’s store, bun’s global cache, or just biting the bullet.
  • Editors that track file paths (not content) sometimes get confused if you open the same file in two worktrees. Restart the editor; it’s fine.

Small workflow change. Big quality-of-life delta.

item.title: Local LLMs on Apple Silicon, one year in
item.description:
I’ve been running language models locally on an M3 Pro for about a year. Not as a replacement for hosted models — the frontier is still far ahead — but as a daily driver for things that don’t need the frontier: code autocomplete, grep-over-my-notes, quick rewrites.

What actually works

  • llama.cpp remains the workhorse. Metal backend is solid. Quantized models in the 8-14B range feel usable on 36 GB of unified memory.
  • ollama is the easy button. I use it for anything I want to share with collaborators without a 40-minute setup dance.
  • mlx from Apple is the speed king on this hardware — ~30% faster tokens/sec on the models I’ve tested, vs equivalent quantizations in llama.cpp.

What doesn’t

  • Anything that promises “GPT-4-class on a laptop.” No. That is not where the Pareto frontier is right now.
  • Fine-tuning locally. Technically possible, practically miserable. Rent a box.
  • 70B+ models. They fit in 36 GB at Q3/Q4 but the speed is in the single-digit tokens/sec range.

What surprised me

How much of my actual usage is “summarize this PDF” or “rephrase this email.” For those, a 12B model is genuinely fine. The upgrade from frontier to local is small; the privacy upgrade is huge.

item.title: Severance, Season 2
item.description:
The aesthetic is doing an incredible amount of work. Every frame is composed like a Wes Anderson cover of a Kafka short story. The plot moves slower than it thinks it does, but the atmosphere carries it.

The “innies vs outies” ethics keep finding new dimensions. I suspect the show is structurally incapable of landing a finale that matches the premise, but the ride is the point.

item.title: Valid Parentheses
item.description:
Problem

Given a string of brackets ()[]{}, determine whether it is valid — every opening bracket has a matching closing bracket, and they are properly nested.

Solution

Classic stack problem. Push opening brackets, pop and compare on closing.

def isValid(s: str) -> bool:
 pairs = {")": "(", "]": "[", "}": "{"}
 stack = []
 for ch in s:
 if ch in "([{":
 stack.append(ch)
 elif not stack or stack.pop() != pairs[ch]:
 return False
 return not stack

Complexity

  • Time: O(n)
  • Space: O(n) — worst case the stack is as long as the input.

item.title: Tunic
item.description:
A small fox with a sword, a cryptic in-game manual written in an invented script, and a world that reveals a second, far deeper layer once you start translating the runes. The first 10 hours feel like Zelda homage; the next 20 feel like the most clever ARG I’ve played in years.

Not for everyone — if “read the manual” isn’t your idea of gameplay, skip. For me, peak satisfaction.

item.title: Reading SICP, slowly
item.description:
Started working through Structure and Interpretation of Computer Programs over the weekend. I bounced off it twice before — once in 2015, once in 2020. This time I’m giving myself permission to go slow. Maybe a chapter a month.

The first time I picked it up, I skimmed the prose and jumped to exercises. Felt like a waste because the exercises only land if you’ve sat with the worldview. This time: read the prose twice, do every exercise, don’t skip.

item.title: X-Files, 2x18 - Fearful Symmetry
item.description:
Epic continuation of Denis Villeneuve’s adaptation. The scale, visuals, and sound design are absolutely stunning. Timothée Chalamet and Zendaya deliver powerful performances.

The way Villeneuve translates Herbert’s complex narrative into pure cinema is masterful. Every frame is meticulously crafted. Hans Zimmer’s score elevates the entire experience.

Best watched in IMAX.

item.title: Two Sum
item.description:
Problem

Given an array of integers nums and an integer target, return indices of the two numbers such that they add up to target.

Solution

The brute force approach would be O(n²), but we can optimize it using a hash table to achieve O(n) time complexity.

def twoSum(nums, target):
 seen = {}
 for i, num in enumerate(nums):
 complement = target - num
 if complement in seen:
 return [seen[complement], i]
 seen[num] = i
 return []

Complexity

  • Time: O(n) - single pass through the array
  • Space: O(n) - hash table storage

Key Insights

Using a hash table allows us to look up complements in constant time, reducing the overall complexity from O(n²) to O(n).

item.title: Heretic
item.description:
I’ve always loved dark fantasy aesthetics, and Heretic remains one of the best representatives of the genre. Built on id Tech 1 (the Doom engine), it perfectly captures that gritty, supernatural atmosphere.

First played this back in the 90s on MS-DOS. Recently revisited it through the Steam release with enhanced graphics, improved music, and proper mouse support. Pure nostalgia.

item.title: On small tools
item.description:
There’s a specific kind of joy in tools that do one thing, do it well, and stay out of your way. fzf is the canonical example — a single fuzzy finder that quietly becomes the glue between everything else.

What makes a good small tool

  • Composable. Speaks stdin/stdout by default. Every feature exposed as a flag, not a config file.
  • Fast. You don’t notice it’s running. If you notice, it’s too slow.
  • Boring. No surprises. No auto-update prompts. No telemetry.
  • Readable source. You can sit down on a weekend and understand the whole thing.

The inverse — the “platform” tool that tries to absorb five adjacent workflows — almost always rots. Either the maintainer burns out, or the feature surface becomes a museum of deprecated ideas.

item.title: Hello, world
item.description:
First post on the rewritten version of this site. The old version was a single-page thing — name, social icons, end of story. I got tired of not having anywhere to write things down, so here we are.
